dryRun.title: Remove the value 3 from 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
rows: prev.next = curr.next, so 2 now points to 4
dryRun.note: To cut a node out you must change the node before it. That is why we carry prev while walking. No element had to move.

think.q:
const a = { val: 1, next: null }
const b = { val: 2, next: null }
a.next = b
b.val = 9
console.log(a.next.val)
why: a.next does not copy b. It holds a reference to the same object, so a change to b is visible through a.next.
Trap: thinking the link stores a copy of the value at the time you linked.

think.q:
const c = { val: 3, next: null }
const b = { val: 2, next: c }
const a = { val: 1, next: b }
let n = 0, cur = a
while (cur) {
  n++
  cur = cur.next
}
console.log(n)
why: The loop visits a, then b, then c. After c, cur becomes null and the loop stops. That is 3 nodes.
The loop condition while (cur) is the standard way to walk to the end of a list.

think.q: You hold node a in the middle of a list and want to insert x right after it. Which pair of lines, in this order, keeps the rest of the list?
why: First point x at the rest of the list (a.next), then point a at x.
In the first option, a.next is already x when the second line runs, so x points to itself and the rest of the list is lost.

think.q: You only hold the head of a singly linked list with n nodes. How long does it take to reach the 50th node?
why: There is no index. You must follow next 49 times, and in the worst case n times. That is O(n).
Trap: remembering that arrays reach any index in O(1). A linked list trades that for cheap inserts and removes.

think.q:
You delete a node with prev.next = curr.next. The node to delete is the head, so prev is null. What prints?

const head = { val: 1, next: { val: 2, next: null } }
let prev = null
try { prev.next = head.next } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: There is no node before the head, so prev.next reads a property of null and throws a TypeError.
Fix: use a dummy node in front of the head, or handle the head case first.

try.task: Write removeValue(head, val). Remove every node whose value equals val and return the new head. Nodes look like { val, next }.
try.hint: Put a dummy node before the head: { val: 0, next: head }. Then you never need a special case for removing the head. Return dummy.next.

checks.t: remove from the middle and end
checks.verify: { const mk = (a) => a.reduceRight((n, v) => ({ val: v, next: n }), null); const arr = (h) => { const o = []; while (h) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next } return o }; assert(JSON.stringify(arr(removeValue(mk([1, 2, 3, 2]), 2))) === "[1,3]", "expected [1,3]") }

{ const mk = (a) => a.reduceRight((n, v) => ({ val: v, next: n }), null); const arr = (h) => { const o = []; while (h) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next } return o }; assert(JSON.stringify(arr(removeValue(mk([2, 2, 1]), 2))) === "[1]", "expected [1]") }
{ const mk = (a) => a.reduceRight((n, v) => ({ val: v, next: n }), null); assert(removeValue(mk([5, 5]), 5) === null, "expected null") }

{ const mk = (a) => a.reduceRight((n, v) => ({ val: v, next: n }), null); const arr = (h) => { const o = []; while (h) { o.push(h.val); h = h.next } return o }; assert(JSON.stringify(arr(removeValue(mk([1, 2]), 9))) === "[1,2]", "list should not change") }

takeaway.key: A linked list has no index: you reach a node by following next, but once you hold a node you can insert or remove without moving anything.
mistakes: Overwriting next before saving it, which loses the rest of the list.
Forgetting the head: there is no prev for it. A dummy node fixes this.
Reading cur.next when cur is null.
Expecting O(1) access by position.

dryRun.title: Is "([)]" balanced?
rows: closing: top is [, but ) needs (. Not balanced
dryRun.note: A closing bracket must match the most recent opening one, which is the top of the stack. Here the top is [, so the string is invalid.

think.q:
const s = []
s.push(1)
s.push(2)
s.push(3)
s.pop()
console.log(s.pop())
why: The first pop removes 3 and throws it away. The second pop returns the next top, which is 2.
Trap: reading the second pop as the first one. Last in, first out.
think.exec:
const s = []
s.push(1)
s.push(2)
s.push(3)
s.pop()
console.log(s.pop())

think.q:
const s = [5, 6]
s.pop()
s.pop()
s.pop()
console.log(s.length, String(s.pop()))
why: The third pop works on an empty array. It does not throw: it returns undefined and the length stays 0.
This is why a bracket checker must test stack.length before it pops.
think.exec:
const s = [5, 6]
s.pop()
s.pop()
s.pop()
console.log(s.length, String(s.pop()))

think.q:
const st = []
for (const ch of 'abc') st.push(ch)
let out = ''
while (st.length) out += st.pop()
console.log(out)
why: Everything pushed comes out in reverse order. That is the core behaviour of a stack.
Reversing a string or a list with a stack is a good first test of LIFO.

think.q: Which task is the most natural fit for a stack?
opts: Undo the last edit in an editor
Serve customers in the order they arrived
Find the shortest path level by level
Look up a user by id
why: Undo always reverses the most recent action first. That is last in, first out.
Serving in arrival order and level-by-level search are first in, first out, which is a queue.

think.q:
This checker only handles ( and ):

function ok(s) {
  const st = []
  for (const ch of s) {
    if (ch === '(') st.push(ch)
    else st.pop()
  }
  return st.length === 0
}

It returns true for ')()', which is not balanced. Why?
opts: A pop on an empty stack does nothing, so an extra ) is silently forgotten
The loop skips the first character
why: The first ) pops an empty stack, which is ignored. Then () balances itself and the stack ends empty.
Fix: if the stack is empty when a closing bracket arrives, return false right away.

try.task: Write evalRPN(tokens). It evaluates an expression in reverse Polish notation: numbers come first, then the operator. Tokens are strings. Supported: + - * /. Division truncates toward zero.
try.hint: Push numbers. On an operator, pop b first and then a, compute a op b, and push the result. The order matters for - and /. The answer is the last item on the stack.

takeaway.key: A stack hands back the most recent unfinished item first: push and pop at the same end, both O(1).
mistakes: Popping an empty stack without checking.
Using shift or unshift as stack operations, which move every element.
Forgetting to check that the stack is empty at the end.
Mixing up the operand order when popping two values.

dryRun.title: Operations on an empty queue
dryRun.note: A went in first, so A comes out first. New items join at the back and never jump ahead.

think.q:
const q = []
q.push('a')
q.push('b')
q.push('c')
console.log(q.shift(), q.length)
why: push adds at the back and shift removes from the front. The first item in is a, so it comes out. Two items remain.
Trap: using pop thinking, which would return c.
think.exec:
const q = []
q.push('a')
q.push('b')
q.push('c')
console.log(q.shift(), q.length)

think.q:
const q = [1]
let out = ''
while (q.length) {
  const x = q.shift()
  out += x
  if (x < 3) q.push(x + 1, x + 1)
}
console.log(out)
why: A queue finishes a whole level before the next one: first 1, then the two 2s, then the four 3s. That is "1" + "22" + "3333".
The option 1233233 is what a stack would give (go deep first).

think.q: You use array.shift() as the dequeue of a queue that holds a million items. Why can this be a problem?
opts: It can cost O(n) per call, because the remaining items are moved
It returns the last item instead of the first
It does not remove the item
why: Removing from the front can force every other item to shift one place. A loop of such calls can become O(n²).
For big queues, keep a head index and move it forward, or use a linked list.

think.q: You must visit the nodes of a tree level by level: all nodes at depth 1 before any node at depth 2. Which structure drives this?
why: Children are added at the back and nodes are taken from the front, so a whole level is finished before the next one starts. This is BFS.
A stack would go deep first instead.

think.q:
const q = []
console.log(String(q.shift()))
why: shift on an empty array returns undefined and does not throw.
So a loop like while (q.length) is the safe way to drain a queue.

try.task: Write binaryNumbers(n). Return the first n binary numbers as strings, starting at "1": "1", "10", "11", "100", .... Use a queue.
try.hint: Start with ["1"] in the queue. Take the front item s, add it to the answer, then enqueue s + "0" and s + "1".

takeaway.key: A queue serves the oldest item first: add at the back, remove from the front. It is the engine of BFS.
mistakes: Using a stack when the order of arrival matters.
Relying on shift() in a huge loop, which can be O(n) per call.
Dequeuing from an empty queue and not handling undefined.
Mixing up the front and the back.

dryRun.title: Find two numbers that add up to 9 in [1, 2, 4, 7, 11]
dryRun.note: Each step throws away one value for good. Because the array is sorted, we never need to check that value again.

think.q:
function pair(a, t) {
  let l = 0, r = a.length - 1
  while (l < r) {
    const s = a[l] + a[r]
    if (s === t) return [l, r]
    if (s < t) l++
    else r--
  }
  return null
}
console.log(pair([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 10).join(","))
why: The pointers start at the two ends. 1 + 9 is already 10, so it returns [0, 4] at once.
Another pair exists (4 + 6), but the function returns the first one it meets.

think.q:
function pair(a, t) {
  let l = 0, r = a.length - 1
  while (l < r) {
    const s = a[l] + a[r]
    if (s === t) return [l, r]
    if (s < t) l++
    else r--
  }
  return null
}
console.log(String(pair([1, 5, 3, 2], 8)))
why: The array is not sorted. 5 + 3 = 8 is a real pair, but the pointers throw values away on a wrong assumption and never see it.
Two pointers that move by "too big / too small" need sorted input.

think.q: Two pointers find a pair with a given sum in a sorted array of n numbers. What are the time and extra space?
why: Each step moves one pointer inward, so there are at most n steps. Only two index variables are used, so extra space is O(1).
Trap: the hash-map solution is also O(n) time, but it costs O(n) space.

think.q: Which task fits two pointers moving from the two ends?
opts: Count word frequencies in a text
Check that a string reads the same backwards, without making a copy
Find the shortest path in a grid
why: Compare the first and last character, then move both pointers inward. No copy and one pass.
The other tasks need counting, searching a graph or merging maps.

think.q: In a sorted array the sum at left = 0, right = 4 is too big. Why can a[4] be thrown away for good?
opts: Even with the smallest remaining partner, a[4] is already too big, so it cannot be in any answer
Pointers are never allowed to move back
why: Every other partner is at least as large as a[0]. If a[0] + a[4] is already too big, any other pair with a[4] is too big too.
This argument is what makes the algorithm correct, not just fast.

try.task: Write sortedSquares(nums). The array is sorted and may contain negative numbers. Return the squares of the numbers, also sorted. Aim for O(n) with two pointers (no sorting at the end).
try.hint: The biggest square is at one of the two ends. Compare Math.abs(nums[l]) with Math.abs(nums[r]), put the bigger square at the end of the result, and fill the result from the back.

takeaway.key: On sorted data, two pointers use the order to discard one candidate per step, so O(n²) becomes O(n).
mistakes: Using it on unsorted data without sorting first.
Moving the wrong pointer after a "too big" or "too small" result.
Using l <= r when the same element must not be used twice.
Forgetting that sorting first costs O(n log n).

dryRun.title: Biggest sum of 3 neighbours in [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
dryRun.note: We never add the three numbers again. We only add the one that enters and remove the one that leaves.

think.q:
const a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
let sum = a[0] + a[1] + a[2], best = sum
for (let i = 3; i < a.length; i++) {
  sum += a[i] - a[i - 3]
  best = Math.max(best, sum)
}
console.log(best)
why: The window sums are 8, 7, 9 and 6. The best is 9, from [5, 1, 3].
Each step uses a[i - 3] because the window holds exactly 3 items: the one that leaves is 3 places behind the new one.
think.exec:
const a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
let sum = a[0] + a[1] + a[2], best = sum
for (let i = 3; i < a.length; i++) {
  sum += a[i] - a[i - 3]
  best = Math.max(best, sum)
}
console.log(best)

think.q:
const a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
let sum = a[0] + a[1] + a[2], best = sum
for (let i = 3; i < a.length; i++) {
  sum += a[i] - a[i - 2]
  best = Math.max(best, sum)
}
console.log(best)
why: The removed index is off by one: a[i - 2] is still inside the window. The sum drifts and the best stays at the first value, 8, instead of 9.
Off-by-one on the leaving item is the most common sliding window bug.
think.exec:
const a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
let sum = a[0] + a[1] + a[2], best = sum
for (let i = 3; i < a.length; i++) {
  sum += a[i] - a[i - 2]
  best = Math.max(best, sum)
}
console.log(best)

think.q: Find the biggest sum of k neighbouring numbers in an array of n numbers using the sliding trick. Time?
why: Each number enters the window once and leaves once. That is O(n) work, no matter how big k is.
Recomputing each window from scratch is O(n * k).

think.q: Which problem is a sliding window problem?
opts: Longest run of characters with at most 2 different letters
Check if a tree is balanced
Count the islands in a grid
Find the k-th smallest value in a BST
why: It asks for the best contiguous segment under a rule. You can grow and shrink a window to keep the rule true.
The other problems are about trees and grids.

think.q: In a variable-size window, when do you move the left edge?
opts: When the window breaks the rule, until it is valid again
Never: only the right edge moves
why: The right edge grows the window. When the window becomes invalid, the left edge shrinks it until the rule holds again.
Use a while loop for this, not an if: one step may not be enough.

try.task: Write longestSubarray(nums, limit). All numbers are positive. Return the length of the longest run of neighbouring numbers whose sum is at most limit. Return 0 if none fits.
try.hint: Move the right edge, adding each number. While the sum is bigger than limit, subtract the left number and move the left edge. After that, the window is valid: update the best length.

takeaway.key: Do not redo the whole window: add the item that enters and remove the item that leaves.
mistakes: Recomputing the whole window each time, which brings back O(n²).
An off-by-one in the index of the item that leaves.
Using if instead of while when shrinking the window.
Updating the best answer before the window is valid again.

flags: The existing lesson texts mention what an interviewer asks. I did not rewrite them.
two-pointers: I used only arrays and big-o as prerequisites. The old text compares with a nested loop, so it does not need hash maps.
The stacks lesson relies on recursion for its call-stack analogy, but recursion comes later in the new order (Unit 4). I did not list it as a prerequisite; the analogy still works without it.
